node.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
node.period_rationale: Berger (1970, 1976), McKillop (1979) and Owram (1980, 1986) fall in "Reorientations, c. 1970–85"; the cultural-history turn (McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999) is period_3.
node.date_label: Berger 1970, 1976 · McKillop 1979 · Owram 1980, 1986 · cultural turn: McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999 · coverage through 2000; post-2000 extension partial

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. Earlier histories of Canadian ideas belong partly to the national tradition; 1970 is the first selected work and 2016 the latest. Neither bounds the field.

node.description: English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history studies how Canadians thought about empire, nation, religion, science and the state, and later how traditions, myths and public memories were made. Carl Berger's The Sense of Power (1970) examined imperialist ideas of Canadian character and mission and argued that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism; his The Writing of Canadian History (1976) made English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject. A. B. McKillop, Marlene Shore and Doug Owram followed ideas into the university, social science, western expansion and the interwar 'service state'. Ramsay Cook's The Regenerators (1985) joined the field to religious history. Critics charged it with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy that said little about what most Canadians thought. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had argued that a field anchored to nationalism left women almost invisible. From the 1990s a cultural history of invention and memory took over much of the ground. Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk (1994) showed tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as a simple folk. Daniel Francis wrote on the 'imaginary Indian' and national myths, and Jonathan Vance on the memory of the First World War. H. V. Nelles, Keith Walden, E. A. Heaman and Ian Radforth studied pageants, exhibitions and royal tours, and Colin Coates and Cecilia Morgan the commemoration of heroines. Yvan Lamonde's social history of ideas in Quebec runs on a separate francophone track.
node.scope_note: English-Canadian by design; Quebec's histoire sociale des idées is a comparison (Lamonde). Intellectual history (ideas, intellectuals, the university) and cultural history (spectacle, myth, memory) are distinct strands with different methods. The religious strand is shared with cdn_religion_reform, postwar identity with cdn_sixties. Editorial observation, not a sourced claim: Indigenous people appear in this field mostly as settler representations (Francis, Heaman), which is a limit to flag in teaching. PhD evidence (2009–2026): engagement with the field's anchor scholars is steady (ratio 1.02; 1.14 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), while its older works are cited less; the classics are ageing, not the field. Owram's 'Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities' (JCS 24:3, 1989; abstract checked, not cited as a source) is a practitioner's self-assessment that also notes the field's nationalist roots and the differing methods of francophone and anglophone writers; it is not treated as a critique.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 1986), Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971), The Regenerators (1985); McKillop, A Disciplined Intelligence (1979), Matters of Mind (1994); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980), The Government Generation (1986); Shore, The Science of Social Redemption (1987); Litt (1992); Vipond (1992); Francis, The Imaginary Indian (1992), National Dreams (1997); McKay, The Quest of the Folk (1994); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Walden (1997); Heaman, The Inglorious Arts of Peace (1999); Nelles, The Art of Nation-Building (1999); Coates and Morgan, Heroines and History (2002); Radforth, Royal Spectacle (2004); Igartua (2006). Critiques: Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History” (1979); Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” (1989). Comparisons: Lamonde, Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); Lears, No Place of Grace (1981).

representative_people.name: Carl Berger
representative_people.context: Studies the ideas of Canadian imperialists (character, mission, loyalism, militarism), which he argued were one form of Canadian nationalism, and makes English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject.
representative_people.works: The Sense of Power (1970); The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 2nd ed. 1986); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983)

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Essays on nationalism and politics, and an intellectual history of late Victorian social criticism that joins the field to religious history; Gauvreau reassesses his account.
representative_people.works: The Maple Leaf Forever (1971); The Regenerators (1985)

representative_people.name: A. B. McKillop
representative_people.context: Victorian critical inquiry and the Ontario university; in 1999 answered Granatstein's charges against academic history.
representative_people.works: A Disciplined Intelligence (1979); Matters of Mind (1994); “Who Killed Canadian History? A View from the Trenches” (1999)

representative_people.name: Marlene Shore
representative_people.context: McGill, the Chicago School and the origins of Canadian social research; title-level only.

representative_people.name: Doug Owram
representative_people.context: Expansionist ideas of the West, and the intellectuals and social scientists who moved into the "service state" and wartime economic management. His later baby-boom history is placed in Canada's 1960s.
representative_people.works: Promise of Eden (1980); The Government Generation (1986)

representative_people.name: Ian McKay
representative_people.context: Shows tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as an antimodern folk, and later the making of the province's public past. Primary placement in the liberal order framework.
representative_people.works: The Quest of the Folk (1994); In the Province of History (2010), with Robin Bates

representative_people.name: H. V. Nelles
representative_people.context: The 1908 Quebec tercentenary as pageantry, "the politics of memory and the theatrics of history".

representative_people.name: Daniel Francis
representative_people.context: Popular historian of the "imaginary Indian" in Canadian culture and of national myths; title-level only here.

representative_people.name: Jonathan F. Vance
representative_people.context: Canada's collective memory of the First World War as cultural rather than military history, and its implications for nationalism.

representative_people.name: Colin M. Coates
representative_people.context: With Cecilia Morgan, the representation of Madeleine de Verchères and Laura Secord; title-level only.
representative_people.works: Heroines and History (2002), with Cecilia Morgan

representative_people.name: Cecilia Morgan
representative_people.context: Heroines and commemoration; metadata only here. Primary placement in women's and gender history.
representative_people.works: Heroines and History (2002), with Colin M. Coates; Commemorating Canada (2016)

representative_people.name: E. A. Heaman
representative_people.context: Nineteenth-century exhibitions as politics, economic development, culture and commodification, including exhibitions of First Nations.

representative_people.name: Keith Walden
representative_people.context: The Toronto Industrial Exhibition and the shaping of a late Victorian urban culture.

representative_people.name: Ian Radforth
representative_people.context: The 1860 royal tour as public spectacle, colonial and national identity, and Britishness.

representative_people.name: Paul Litt
representative_people.context: Culture, mass culture and the Massey Commission; title-level only.
representative_people.works: The Muses, the Masses, and the Massey Commission (1992)

representative_people.name: Mary Vipond
representative_people.context: The first decade of Canadian broadcasting; metadata only.

representative_people.name: José E. Igartua
representative_people.context: Traces the dissolution of English Canada's British self-definition into a civic, rights-based identity, 1945–71. Primary placement in Canada's 1960s.

representative_people.name: Yvan Lamonde
representative_people.context: Francophone counterpart: a social history of ideas in Quebec, presented as intellectual history in Mens. Primary placement in Quebec historiography.
representative_people.works: Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); “L’histoire sociale des idées comme histoire intellectuelle” (2001)

representative_people.name: T. J. Jackson Lears
representative_people.context: American comparison for the antimodernism strand: middle- and upper-class Americans' search for authentic experience, which in his account accommodated them to corporate capitalism. Heavily co-cited with McKay's Quest of the Folk in Canadian PhDs; McKay's own use of Lears is unchecked.

representative_people.name: Clarence Karr
representative_people.context: Faults English-Canadian intellectual history for seeking a national mind, framing everything as crisis, and a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' centred on academics, journalists and clergy.

representative_people.name: Susan Mann Trofimenkoff
representative_people.context: Feminist critique: a field anchored to nationalism and present-minded concern with national unity implied that women were 'virtually non-existent'.

strands.title: Ideas of empire, nation and history
strands.focus: Imperialist and nationalist thought (Berger reads imperialism as one form of Canadian nationalism), and English-Canadian historical writing as an object of study.
strands.works: Berger (1970, 1976); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971)

strands.title: Victorian thought, science, religion and the university
strands.focus: Critical inquiry, science and faith, the university and social criticism in Victorian Canada; the religious strand continues in cdn_religion_reform.

strands.title: Intellectuals, social science and the state
strands.focus: Expansionist ideas, the social sciences and the intellectuals who entered the "service state", the Rowell-Sirois inquiry and wartime economic management.

strands.title: Antimodernism and the invented folk
strands.focus: Tourism, folklore and handicrafts refashion a region as an antimodern folk; later, the making of a public past and its cultural politics of whiteness. Comparison: American antimodernism (Lears).
strands.works: McKay (1994); McKay and Bates (2010); comparison: Lears, No Place of Grace (1981)

strands.title: Exhibition, pageant and royal tour
strands.focus: Public spectacle as politics, commerce and identity: exhibitions, the 1908 tercentenary, the 1860 royal tour.

strands.title: Myth, image, memory and commemoration
strands.focus: National myths, the image of the "Indian", war memory and commemorated heroines.
strands.works: Francis (1992, 1997); Vance (1997); Coates and Morgan (2002); Morgan (2016)

strands.title: Culture, media and the state
strands.focus: Broadcasting and the Massey Commission: high, mass and national culture as policy questions. Title-level only.

strands.title: Postwar national identity
strands.focus: The end of British Canada and the rise of a civic, rights-based identity; continues in Canada's 1960s.

strands.title: Francophone counterpart: histoire sociale des idées
strands.focus: Quebec's social history of ideas runs on a separate track with its own journal (Mens); a comparison, not a branch of the English-Canadian field.

strands.title: Critiques of the field
strands.focus: Feminist and methodological critiques of English-Canadian intellectual history: nationalism and the absence of women (Trofimenkoff), an elitist group-biography method and a search for the national mind (Karr). Rarely cited in recent PhDs.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry (period_2), with the cultural turn in period_3 and a partial post-2000 extension.

proposed_source_records.title: Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970; 2nd ed. 2013).
proposed_source_records.citation: Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970; 2nd ed. 2013).

verification.note: Contents read (2nd ed.): "Men", "Canada First", "The Loyalist Tradition", "Progress and Liberty", "The Canadian Character", "Critique of the Republic", "Social Criticism and Reform", "Mission", "Militarism". The book's thesis is not read; the first-edition year (1970 vs 1971) should be confirmed. Thesis (added 2026-10-12, partly verified): Berger's formulation that Canadian imperialism was one variety (Stamp) or version (Cook) of Canadian nationalism is known from two later scholars' quotations and the UTP publisher copy ('significantly influenced by its leading advocates' belief in nationalism'); the exact word and page in the 1970 introduction are unchecked, so the draft paraphrases and does not quote.

verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Argues Canadian intellectual history, anchored to nationalism and present-minded interest in national unity, implied 'that women are virtually non-existent'; notes most intellectual historians were men and that women's history grew from social history in isolation from it; urges attention to feminist ideas and women's part in forming ideology. Examples mostly French-Canadian; critique covers Cook, Berger and Shortt. Special issue on intellectual history. Karr (1989, n. 6) cites it with the issue misgiven as 93.

verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Analyses the field's 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis' and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160); group biography after Berger's Sense of Power focuses on 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' (p. 169), leaving little known of what the population thought. Names Berger, McKillop, Cook, Shortt, Levitt, Allen and Francis; calls the books 'excellent studies within their self-imposed context'.

proposed_relationships.relationship: A national field within intellectual history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Titles name the field's objects (Canadian thought, intellectuals and the state, historical writing); Gauvreau's Evangelical Century was presented as transforming "the way Canadian intellectual history is interpreted". Comparison: the Canadian field developed largely apart from the contextualist and conceptual programmes in the atlas entry; no checked source links them.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Canadian studies of collective memory, pageantry and the public past
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Vance studies Canada's collective memory of the First World War; Nelles "the politics of memory" at the 1908 tercentenary; McKay and Bates the making of Nova Scotia's public past. A contribution of case studies, not a claim that the field originated memory studies.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Ideas and representations of Canadian nationhood
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Berger's chapters on Canada First and "The Canadian Character"; Vance on war memory and Canadian nationalism; Igartua on the shift from ethnic to civic national identity. Comparison: the Canadian works rarely engage the modernist theory debates of the atlas entry in the checked pages.

Heaman's "Exhibition Culture" and commodification, Walden's exhibition and urban culture, and Radforth's public spectacle share the new cultural history's attention to representation and performance. Comparison only: no checked page cites the new cultural historians.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Tourism, heritage and the making of public pasts
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: McKay and Bates trace tourism/history and the cultural politics of whiteness in Nova Scotia; McKay's Quest of the Folk shows the tourism industry refashioning regional identity. These study public history as a subject rather than practising it.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Berger's historiography of English-Canadian historical writing
proposed_relationships.map_label: Writing the history of Canadian history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976; subtitle "Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970") is the standard analysis of the tradition the proposed national-tradition entry describes (groups.json scope). Title-level evidence only; the book's chapters were not checked. Target is proposed.
Cook's Regenerators belongs to both fields; Gauvreau's Evangelical Century reassesses Cook as intellectual history. PhD context: 34 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 3.5). Both endpoints proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Intellectual history answers the liberal order framework
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: McNairn's chapter is titled "In Hope and Fear: Intellectual History, Liberalism, and the Liberal Order Framework"; McKay and Heaman write in both fields. PhD context: 43 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 3.5). Title-level only; both endpoints proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Postwar national identity and the generation of the 1960s
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Igartua traces English Canada's "other Quiet Revolution" in national identity, 1945–71; Owram moves from intellectuals and the state (1986) to the baby boom (1996). PhD context: 40 PhDs engage both drafts (lift 2.5). Both endpoints proposed.

McKillop argues that Granatstein "miscasts the role of the scholar as citizen" and that his narrow national history is itself political legitimation. One contributor's intervention, not the whole field's position. Target is proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: English-Canadian and Quebec histories of ideas and commemoration
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Lamonde's histoire sociale des idées is Quebec's counterpart; Nelles studies Quebec's tercentenary and Coates and Morgan Madeleine de Verchères. PhD context: 16 of 27 PhDs citing Lamonde (2000) are at francophone universities, against 2 of 48 for Berger (1976). Target is proposed.
Vance's Death So Noble "deals with cultural history more than military history" while treating the war's memory. Comparison only; target is proposed.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: No atlas entry for American antimodernism, so no edge. Lears is now a comparison row in the roster (publisher description checked; 15 of 60 PhDs citing The Quest of the Folk also cite No Place of Grace, lift 10.2); McKay's use of Lears is unchecked.
No checked source places Canadian intellectual historians in the Cambridge School.
Francis and Heaman study representations of Indigenous people; a relationship would need Indigenous-authored or critical sources not checked here.

open_questions: One entry or two? Intellectual history (Berger, McKillop, Owram, Shore) and cultural history of spectacle and memory (McKay, Nelles, Vance, Heaman) have different methods; the draft keeps them together as strands, following groups.json.

Berger's Sense of Power is usually summarized by its argument that imperialism was a form of Canadian nationalism; that formulation is not checked here and is kept out of the description. Confirm from the book's introduction before using it.
Engagement (PhDs citing two or more listed works) falls from 13.2% (2009–14) to 8.4% (2020–26). Is that the cultural turn ageing, or a coverage artefact?
Should Lears's American antimodernism be noted as a comparison? It is heavily co-cited with McKay but unchecked.
No checked critique of the field as a whole was found. Do you want one sought (for example social historians' charges of elitism, or Palmer on the cultural turn)?

question_resolutions.summary: Kept as one entry with two strands: the intellectual- and cultural-history literatures overlap (lift 3.0) less than several pairs kept separate, so the data neither require a merge nor justify a split.

The description, Berger's roster row and the empire strand now attribute to Berger the argument that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism, paraphrased without quotation marks; the word ('variety' or 'version') and page in the 1970 introduction remain unchecked and are flagged in cic_berger_1970.

The scope note and evidence.json now describe the field as steady (anchor engagement ratio 1.02; panel 1.14) with its older works less cited; the earlier 13.2% to 8.4% fall is recorded as a decline in specific older works, not in the field.

Added T. J. Jackson Lears as a comparison row (No Place of Grace, 1981; publisher description checked against the University of Chicago Press page; QID Q7668351 from the scholar packet) and to the antimodernism strand. No edge, since the atlas has no antimodernism entry; McKay's use of Lears is unchecked.

Added a critique sentence anchored on Karr 1989 (Acadiensis 18:2, 158–74) and Trofimenkoff 1979 (Canadian Literature 83, 7–20), both read in full, with critic rows and a critiques strand. Palmer 1990 and Owram 1989 are not used as critiques (Owram noted in the scope note as a self-assessment); Gauvreau 2010 not added (review only). Low PhD uptake recorded in evidence.json and NOTES.
